cse-2020-cs-2.approach: Each call replaces n by its a-th root. Count how many roots it takes to bring n down to b by working with log_b n.

steps.title: Solve for k
steps.body: $n^{1/a^k} = b \iff \frac{\log_b n}{a^k} = 1 \iff a^k = \log_b n \iff k = \log_a \log_b n$.

steps.title: Result
steps.body: $T(n) = k + T(b) = \log_a\log_b n + 1 = \Theta(\log_a \log_b n)$.

A single log would come from division (n/ab), not from taking roots.
Swaps the bases. The outer log counts the a-th roots, so its base is a.
Since a and b are ω(1) (they grow), the bases matter, so log₂log₂ n is not the same order.

cse-2020-cs-2.shortcut: Substitute $m = \log_b n$: then $S(m) = S(m/a) + 1$, which gives $S(m) = \log_a m$.

cse-2020-cs-10.approach: Build a DPDA to show L is a DCFL. Then show that a top-down LL(k) parser would have to decide, after seeing only k symbols, whether b's will follow a long run of a's, which it cannot do.

steps.title: L is a DCFL
steps.body: DPDA: push each a while staying in an accepting state (this accepts aⁿ, including ε). On the first b, switch to a popping state: pop one a for each b, and accept when the stack is empty after the b's. No guessing is needed, so L is deterministic CF. **I is true**, which makes **II false**.

steps.title: Not LL(k)
steps.body: An LL(k) parser must pick the production for the start symbol from the first $k$ symbols alone. For $a^{k+1}$ and $a^{k+1}b^{k+1}$ the lookahead $a^k$ is the same, yet the derivations differ: one only generates a's, the other must pair each a with a b. This holds for every $k$, so L is not LL(k). **III is true**.

steps.title: Conclusion
